title: How to become a star
caption: The dark cloud Barnard 68, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
celestial: B 68, Barnard 68 · constellation Ophiuchus · about 500 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Official ESO press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This color composite shows the dark cloud Barnard 68, combining images taken in visible and near-infrared light. The observations were made in March 1999 with the 8.2-meter VLT Antu telescope and its FORS1 multimode instrument.
In both visible and near-infrared light, this small cloud lets nothing through. Dust particles inside it block the light of the stars behind, so the cloud itself looks completely dark.

Dark clouds like this are cold, dense concentrations of gas and dust, and they are the kind of places where new stars can eventually form, which is why the release was titled How to become a star. Dust blocks shorter wavelengths of light more strongly than longer ones, so astronomers often study such clouds by comparing how much starlight gets through at different colors. The official caption offers few further details about this particular cloud.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (6.83 x 6.83 arcminutes) and distance (500 light years), the frame spans roughly 1 × 1 light-years. Its light set out about 500 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This composite from FORS1 on the Very Large Telescope combines visible and near-infrared images through B, V and I filters. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
filters: 440 nm · Optical B (Very Large Telescope FORS1)
557 nm · Optical V (Very Large Telescope FORS1)
768 nm · Infrared I (Very Large Telescope FORS1)
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared, invisible to the eye. Even so, at these wavelengths the cloud remains completely dark.
